title: M-Ch-L

cards: A friend borrowed some cash in the spring. It's autumn now. Neither of you mentions it, and both of you remember it every time you split a check.
There are three ways this ends. Somebody pays. Somebody nags.
Or the lender says, out loud, forget it, we're square, and means it. That third ending has a name in the language of the rabbis: mechilah.
It's the word for waiving a claim, and the word Jews use, especially before Yom Kippur, when they ask one another for forgiveness. Mem, chet, lamed: M-Ch-L.

teach.b: Yesterday's root was pardon. Today's is quieter and more practical: mechilah is giving up something you're owed. Turn it four ways.
First, the ledger. In the rabbis' legal language, if someone owes you and you say machul lach, it's waived, the debt is gone. Nobody pays it back.
You simply stop holding the paper. Second, the question. Two days ago came the Mishnah's line: between people, Yom Kippur waits until they make peace.
Mechilah is what one person asks the other in that moment. Not, do you feel better? Not, was it fine?

teach.h: THE QUESTION: WILL YOU WAIVE IT?

teach.b: Third, the asker's side. The Talmud discusses the person you hurt who won't grant it, and teaches that you keep trying, sincerely and with others present, but there is a limit. Asking for forgiveness is a duty.

Forcing it is not. Fourth, the night. In traditional prayer books, the bedtime Shema, which you met on day one hundred twenty, opens with a short paragraph forgiving anyone who wronged you, in word or in deed.
Every night, a small mechilah before sleep.
Look back at this week: calling out, books, aiming, missing the mark, covering, pardon, and now waiving. One long walk from what's written to what's owed.

how: Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally seek out people they may have wronged and ask for mechilah, forgiveness, and traditional prayer books include a declaration of forgiveness for others at the start of the bedtime Shema.

o: a root for illness, the kind that lingers for a season
a root for erasing, as a scribe scrapes off a word
a root for waiving what you're owed, a kind of forgiving

s: mechilah means the debt gets paid back in full
it means the one who is owed stops holding the claim. nobody pays it back.
in traditional prayer books, the bedtime Shema opens with forgiving others
a person declares that they forgive anyone who wronged them, in word or in deed.
the Talmud says you may pressure someone forever until they forgive
you keep asking sincerely, but there is a limit. asking is a duty; forcing is not.

games.q: it's late, and you open a traditional prayer book to the bedtime Shema. what comes first?
o: a list of the day's mistakes.
a declaration forgiving anyone who wronged you.
a request that others forgive you.
games.why: before sleep, a small mechilah: you forgive anyone who wronged you, in word or in deed.

practice: Bring to mind something small someone owes you, money, an apology, a returned favor, a call they never made, and if what comes up is a deep hurt, choose something smaller for today.
Notice how long you've carried it, then try the bedtime words silently in your own voice: whatever this person owes me, I let it go.
You don't have to tell them or pretend it was fine; just put the paper down, and if you pray, bring their name into the quiet.

wordCard.voice: M-Ch-L. Mem, chet, lamed: the root of mechilah, waiving what you're owed, and the forgiveness Jews ask of one another before Yom Kippur. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: waiving a claim; forgiveness between people.

carryVoice: Your line: let it go. Waiving a debt isn't pretending it was fine. Sleep well tonight.

sources.ref: Bedtime Shema (Kriat Shema al haMitah), opening declaration of forgiveness
